decisions.title: Ship Dr. Markdown as a local Wails desktop app (superseded by own-the-host)
decisions.context: The application is targeted at macOS and embeds frontend assets through Wails rather than serving a website.
decisions.decision: Use Wails to host the editor UI locally and bind native Go document operations into the frontend.
consequences: The frontend can remain static assets embedded in the binary
Native file dialogs and close guards live in Go
Browser-only behavior must be suppressed or replaced where it leaks into the desktop UX
SUPERSEDED 2026-08-10 by own-the-host. Kept because the reasoning still holds — a local desktop app with embedded assets and native Go file operations — and only the framework underneath changed.

decisions.title: Keep filesystem access behind the Go API
decisions.context: The frontend shell runs in a webview and should not directly read or write local files.
decisions.decision: Route open, save, save-as, dirty-state, and unsaved-change guard behavior through the host-bound Go methods.
consequences: E2E tests can stub bridge methods without native dialogs
Document IO stays testable as a Go package
The frontend owns editor state but not filesystem writes

decisions.title: Write saved documents atomically
decisions.context: Markdown saves should not leave a truncated target file if the process fails mid-write.
decisions.decision: Write content to a same-directory temp file, fsync, close, and rename over the target path.
consequences: Save behavior is covered by focused Go unit tests
Write failures remove the temp file when possible

decisions.title: Use vendored editor bundles
decisions.context: The frontend is currently static assets under frontend/dist and does not depend on an npm build at runtime.
decisions.decision: Use vendored Milkdown Crepe, Highlight.js, Mermaid, and editor bundles through small local adapters.
consequences: The app can build through Wails without npm install/build commands
Editor capabilities are limited to what the vendored bundles expose
Raw and Split source highlighting plus fenced-code highlighting are backed by the shared Highlight.js adapter
Mermaid assistant previews and Mermaid fenced-block rendering are backed by the shared Mermaid adapter
Raw hide-markers still require a future editable token/decoration layer

decisions.title: Do not render decorative enabled controls
decisions.context: The current screen is being brought to functional parity before moving through concept screens.
decisions.decision: Visible enabled controls must either mutate state, call a native bridge, or be removed until their subsystem exists.
consequences: Preview, Share, Export, Split, fake docs rows, and unsupported marker hiding are deferred rather than faked
E2E tests enforce that shell buttons are backed

decisions.title: Persist backed runtime settings natively
decisions.context: The Settings concept includes application preferences, Sync, Git, extensions, and markdown flavour choices. The implemented settings slice now has a native JSON preference store, but the broader Sync, Git, Extensions, and Markdown flavour subsystems remain unimplemented.
decisions.decision: Persist backed Editor and Appearance settings through the Wails Go API while keeping unbacked settings categories disabled.
consequences: Settings stage changes in the frontend and write the saved preference envelope through the native bridge
Theme, document font, document font size, system-derived code font, code ligatures, raw soft wrap, and raw line numbers survive app relaunch
Markdown flavour, Sync, Git, Extensions, Preview, Share, Export, and Help settings remain absent until their backing subsystems exist

decisions.title: Copy imported images beside the document and reject unsaved documents
decisions.context: Markdown on disk is the source of truth and must stay portable. An image imported into a document that has no path on disk could only be referenced by an absolute local path, which breaks the moment the document moves.
decisions.decision: Imported images are copied into <document-name>.assets/ beside the markdown file and referenced by relative path, with deterministic -1/-2 collision suffixes. Imports into an unsaved document are rejected before the picker opens, so the user is never asked to choose a file the import cannot accept.
consequences: Images stay portable when the document and its asset folder move together
A document must be saved before images can be inserted
Moving the markdown file without its .assets folder produces missing assets

decisions.title: Inline document-relative image assets as data URIs
decisions.context: Markdown resolves relative image paths against the document on disk, but the webview resolves them against the Wails asset-server origin. A copied asset therefore never renders from its relative path, and the OS print/PDF path cannot resolve document-relative paths at all.
decisions.decision: Every rendering surface (formatted editor, split preview, print/export root) routes local image sources through the Go asset loader, which returns the bytes as a base64 data URI. A missing asset returns no data and is marked as a visible broken state instead of failing the render.
consequences: Imported images render in the editor and survive print/PDF export
Lost assets are visibly broken rather than silently blank
Large images are held in memory as base64 for the lifetime of the render

decisions.title: Express image sizing as an tag and keep the markdown form otherwise
decisions.context: CommonMark has no image sizing syntax. The editor already emits inline HTML for highlight (<mark>), so inline HTML is an established convention in this document model.
decisions.decision: An image with no width stays as portable ![alt](path). Setting a width rewrites it to ; clearing the width restores the markdown form. Only src, alt, and width are ever emitted, and only those attributes are read back when rendering a document-supplied tag.
consequences: The HTML form only appears where it carries information markdown cannot express
Sized images depend on the renderer supporting inline HTML
Event-handler attributes in an opened document are dropped rather than rendered

decisions.title: Recover from unreadable preferences rather than failing startup
decisions.context: Preferences Load treated a missing file as benign but a malformed one as fatal. That error reached a boot path with no catch, so a truncated preferences.json left the user a blank window with no in-app recovery. The store that wrote the file non-atomically was the same store that could not read it back.
decisions.decision: A malformed preferences file is quarantined alongside the original and Load returns empty defaults. The frontend additionally catches at boot, so no boot-time bridge call can prevent the editor mounting. Preferences and documents now share one atomic write primitive in internal/atomicfile, removing the source of the truncation.
consequences: The application always starts, even with an unreadable preference store
A corrupt file is preserved for diagnosis instead of being silently discarded
Preferences silently reset to defaults after corruption, which the quarantined file makes discoverable
Documents and preferences cannot drift apart on write durability

decisions.title: Give the markdown document domain a single owner, separate from the editor adapter
decisions.context:
Five fidelity defects were fixed in two days and every one lived at the seam where the vendored editor's output is patched back into the user's markdown; one grew the file by a duplicated footnote definition on every save, without bound. Five preservations (frontmatter,
sentinels, link references, image alt text, trailing newline) are the same concept implemented five ad-hoc ways, with state on WysiwygEditor private fields and a hand-ordered restore chain, so adding one is a three-place edit and nothing can enumerate or uniformly test them. More broadly, app.js is 2835 lines and 189 top-level functions spanning about ten domains, and app.go is both the Wails binding surface and the application logic behind it. A large part of this product is pure string-to-string markdown logic sitting in the outermost circle, which matters here because e2e is the ONLY frontend coverage, takes about 210 seconds, and has a nondeterministic browser launch.
decisions.decision: Adopt inward-pointing domain boundaries. Introduce a fidelity preservation port — name, capture(original), restore(serialized, state) — with a registry module owning the ordering, so adding a preservation is one file plus one registry line and editor.js returns to owning only the Crepe lifecycle. Then move the pure markdown logic (command transforms, table operations, fence operations, image tokens, link safety) out of app.js into domain modules taking and returning strings. Then lift open, save, resolve-unsaved and asset import out of app.go into use-case types, leaving App as a thin adapter; the injected ports already exist and do not change. No Node toolchain, no framework, no DI container; pure modules are exercised through the existing chromedp harness by importing them directly. internal/* is untouched — it already has single ownership and is the model the rest follows.
consequences: Phase 1 LANDED 2026-08-09: six compensations moved into frontend/dist/src/fidelity/ behind two ports, with a registry owning both orders. editor.js went from 286 lines owning the Crepe lifecycle AND five preservations to 118 owning only the lifecycle, and a test now fails if it names any preservation. Every gate stayed green and UNCHANGED through all eight steps.

Phase 2 LANDED 2026-08-09: 360 lines of pure markdown logic moved from app.js into frontend/dist/src/markdown/ across six modules — tables, fences, images, links, text, commands. Five were leaves with zero dependencies on the rest of app.js, measured from the call graph before the move. app.js went 2835 -> 2452 lines. Every existing test stayed green and unchanged.

Phase 3 LANDED 2026-08-09: the open-document session moved to internal/session — tabs, dirty state and the on-disk baseline — with their invariants tested directly rather than through the binding surface. Scope was deliberately narrowed from this decision's section 3: the use-case-TYPE split was NOT done, because newAppWithDependencies already injects every port and the save path was already testable with zero infrastructure, so it would have moved code without making anything newly safe. The move surfaced two things the plan missed: the loop deciding which tab a write lands on was duplicated verbatim across save and open (now AdoptPath), and the unsynced-dirty flag must re-check the tab count at read time rather than trust it from write time.
Fidelity gains one owner and one shape — the thing whose absence produced five defects in two days.

The bulk of the product's logic becomes verifiable without booting a browser per behaviour, which matters because e2e is the only frontend coverage, runs ~210s, and has a nondeterministic browser launch.
Adding a fidelity preservation becomes one file plus one registry line, instead of a three-place edit with hand-ordered restore steps.

Sequencing is fidelity first (highest defect density, smallest blast radius, already fenced by two behavioural gates), pure markdown domain second (larger, and partly bootstraps its own safety net), Go use cases last (dependency inversion already exists, so deferring costs clarity rather than safety).
Main risk: the second step is a wide edit to a 2835-line file whose only coverage boots a browser, so it must land as a sequence of small green extractions rather than one change.
Judging criterion: the byte-identical corpus and the 49-construct survey must stay green and UNCHANGED throughout. A step needing either gate edited to pass has changed behaviour and is wrong.
PROPOSED pending maintainer review; recorded as planned, not accepted. Full reasoning in docs/decisions/2026-08-09-domain-ownership-and-boundaries.md.

decisions.title: Own the macOS host instead of depending on an application framework
decisions.context: Wails met every stated requirement, and was rejected on the relationship rather than on capability. Three maintainer objections: no control over the internals of one of the largest pieces of the application; dependence on an upstream bug-resolution schedule, which issue #61 demonstrated concretely — a panicking bound call left the frontend promise unsettled forever, with no downstream fix available and none in v2.14.0; and a 151-module trust surface. A fourth objection, that the framework involved TCP between Go and the frontend, was CHECKED AND REFUTED and is recorded so it is not derived again: both net.Listen sites in v3/pkg sit behind the server and mcp build tags.
decisions.decision: Write the macOS host against AppKit and WebKit directly, behind the hostPort boundary already established. Measured before committing: a working host is the size of the boundary it replaces, not the size of the framework — Wails' macOS layer is 5,116 lines, but it buys a tray, custom chrome and a dev server this application does not use.
consequences: No third-party dependency remains in the running application
A panicking bound call REJECTS the frontend promise, closing #61 with no upstream involved
The menu bar became ours to build, and its absence removed Cmd-C, Cmd-V, Cmd-X, Cmd-A and Cmd-Q until it was found
Bound-method dispatch is generated from app.go, so a renamed method is a compile error rather than a silent no-op
Windows and Linux have no host at all; neither was ever built under the framework either
Host verification drives a native window, so it cannot run in CI and is a manual step on a Mac

decisions.title: Let the vendored editor own fenced code blocks
decisions.context: Code blocks could not be edited in Formatted mode, which contradicts the rule the editor exists to serve, and they shipped that way in v0.5.1. The cause was measured rather than inferred: esm.sh resolves the bare specifier `codemirror` inside the Crepe bundle to CodeMirror 5, whose namespace has no `basicSetup` export, so the code-block node view built its CodeMirror extension set with an undefined entry and EditorState.create threw. The throw happened inside the IntersectionObserver callback that upgrades a block, after the node view had already set `initialized = true`, so it was never retried and every block stayed on a placeholder inside a `contenteditable="false"` wrapper. The app had compensated by drawing its own static chrome and Highlight.js output over that placeholder, which made the block look deliberate.
decisions.decision: Patch the vendored bundle to drop the undefined extension, and let the editor's own code-block node view render, highlight and edit fenced blocks. Remove the app's in-editor code-block pass entirely. Supply mermaid diagrams to that node view through its preview hook, so a diagram renders in place and its source stays editable behind a toggle. Keep the app's shell for the preview and print surfaces, where nothing else draws the block.
consequences: Code blocks are editable in Formatted mode, verified by a gate that types real keystrokes and requires them in the document's markdown rather than asserting an element exists.
Mermaid diagrams became editable in place for the first time; previously they rendered but could only be changed by leaving Formatted mode, which was the same rule violation in a different construct.
A whole class of race disappeared. The app's pass and the node view both mutated the same DOM, so whichever ran second won, and the block was left either inert or undecorated.

The language picker, copy button and language list are the editor's, so the app's hover language tool and right-click language menu were removed. The contextual controls bar remains a second route to the same change.

KNOWN DEVIATION: the editor's picker writes a language's DISPLAY name into the fence, so choosing Python through it produces "```Python" where every other route in this app writes "```python". Markdown treats info strings case-insensitively so nothing renders differently, but it is inconsistent with the normalization this project applies everywhere else. Asserted in e2e/code_block_language_test.go so it cannot drift unnoticed.

Wiring the separately vendored codemirror.bundle.mjs was measured and REFUTED as a repair: it puts a second copy of @codemirror/state on the page and CodeMirror rejects the result with "Unrecognized extension value in extension set". That bundle had been fetched and digest-pinned while imported by nothing, and was deleted once it was shown to have no possible use.

The mis-resolution cannot be fixed at the fetch either. @milkdown/crepe declares `codemirror: ^6.0.1`, so this is an esm.sh bug; ?deps= and ?alias= are ignored because the es2022 path is a prebuilt artifact, and jsdelivr's +esm build resolves correctly but emits 46 external imports, which no self-contained CSP-'self' asset server can load.

What the dropped extension carried, measured in the built app rather than read off basicSetup's feature list: line numbers and the fold gutter, bracket auto-closing, and autocompletion are gone. Undo is NOT gone — the node view forwards CodeMirror updates into ProseMirror transactions, so the document's own history answers Cmd-Z inside a code block. Multi-line editing, highlighting and the default keymap all work.

decisions.title: Mac App Store distribution is deferred; Developer ID notarization is the path
decisions.context: Apple Developer Program enrolment costs $99 a year and covers both distribution paths, which invites the assumption that notarizing for direct download also permits publishing to the Mac App Store. It does not. They are different paths: different certificates, a .pkg rather than a .dmg, App Review in place of notarization, and the App Sandbox is mandatory rather than optional. Measured against the source at 1.6.3, the sandbox blocks three things this application does. It reads files the user never picked, because assets.LoadForDocument resolves a relative image path against the document's own directory and reads it — opening notes.md grants notes.md, not notes.assets/figure.png beside it. It writes beside the document, creating <document>.assets/ on image import. And OpenRecentDocument opens a recorded path with no picker, which under the sandbox requires security-scoped bookmarks; internal/preferences stores plain path strings and has no concept of one.
decisions.decision: Defer Mac App Store distribution. Ship notarized direct download via a Developer ID certificate, which delivers the actual objective — a stranger downloads the application and it opens — for $99 and an afternoon, with no sandbox rework and no review queue. What the App Store adds beyond that is discovery and payments, both worth close to nothing for an MIT-licensed editor with no price and no marketing surface.
consequences: Cannot be listed on the Mac App Store without reworking asset resolution and the recents system around security-scoped bookmarks, threading the bookmark lifecycle through the preference store and the asset manager.
Every release would additionally wait on App Review, on Apple's schedule.
Behaviour a user can see would change: an assets folder never individually granted needs re-authorising, and a recents entry whose bookmark went stale needs re-picking.
Revisit if paid distribution or App Store discovery becomes worth funding that work.
Not before source-preserving editing lands: the WYSIWYG re-serialization blocker is the larger constraint, and sandbox work ahead of it buys reach rather than correctness.

decisions.title: One parser renders the preview and the print surface, behind an allowlist sanitizer
decisions.context: The split preview and print/PDF export shared a 43-line renderer built from regular expressions over lines. Enumerated against sixteen ordinary constructs, sixteen rendered wrongly: a GFM table became paragraphs of pipe characters, an ordered list lost its numbering, nested lists flattened, task lists kept literal brackets, emphasis inside a heading or blockquote stayed as asterisks, and a hard-wrapped paragraph split in two. The editor surface was correct throughout, so the two disagreed about the same document. The weight is on print rather than preview: a PDF leaves the application, reaches a reader who never sees the source, and cannot be corrected afterwards.
decisions.decision: Render both surfaces with vendored markdown-it plus markdown-it-footnote and markdown-it-task-lists, configured html:true and linkify:false, and pass every rendered tree through an allowlist sanitizer before it is inserted. markdown-it's own validateLink is turned off so that the sanitizer is the single authority on which URLs survive.
consequences: All sixteen constructs now render correctly on both surfaces, verified construct-by-construct rather than by markup comparison.

html:true is what makes the sanitizer mandatory rather than defensive: it hands untrusted document bytes to a DOM that shares an origin with the native bindings. The renderer it replaced was safe from this only by accident, because it emitted text nodes and never built hostile markup into elements at all.

Disabling validateLink is not a relaxation. markdown-it refuses four schemes by denylist; the sanitizer runs an allowlist, so everything markdown-it refused is still refused. What changes is that the refusal now happens where it can be seen and recorded: a link dissolved during parsing leaves no element, so nothing downstream could tell a refused link from a document that never had one.

Fenced blocks render through a slot rather than as HTML, because the diagram and the code-block chrome are event listeners as much as markup, and those belong to the application rather than to the renderer.

A document embedding raw inline <svg> now shows nothing for it, and document-authored id and style attributes are dropped. Both are real fidelity losses accepted deliberately: inline SVG is a second sanitizer's worth of rules, and a document-authored id can answer a getElementById query meant for the application.

decisions.title: Split shows the real editor, not a second rendering of the document
decisions.context: Split mode's formatted pane was a preview drawn by a separate renderer. That renderer disagreed with the editor about sixteen ordinary markdown constructs, carried its own typography scale — h1 at 32px against the editor's 36px, its own blockquote and pre styling — and fell further behind every time the editor gained something it did not have. It also made the pane read-only, so the formatted half of split was the one surface in a WYSIWYG editor you could not type into. Two renderings of one document is the defect; fixing the renderer only narrows the gap.
decisions.decision: Move the editor ELEMENT into the split formatted pane on entering split mode, and back to the document card on leaving. The editor instance is not rebuilt to move it: reparenting a live ProseMirror tree preserves its content, editability and serialization, which was measured before the design was built on it.
consequences: The two surfaces cannot drift apart in typography, highlighting or construct coverage, because there is only one of them. The second typography scale was deleted rather than corrected.
The formatted pane is editable, which is what the rest of the product already promised.

Both panes are live editors over one document, so each one's refresh fires the other's change handler. An explicit authority — the pane the user last pressed a key or pointer in — decides which one wins; without it the pane being typed into is rebuilt from the pane merely echoing it, and the caret jumps every keystroke.

The authority is driven by keydown and pointerdown rather than focus. Focus was tried and measured wrong: the editor already holds focus when split opens, so focusin never fires for the formatted pane, and focus is also the one signal a rebuild raises by itself.
Rebuilding the formatted pane is rebuilding a real editor, so it waits for a pause in typing rather than running per keystroke, and re-checks the authority when it fires.
markdown/render.js now has exactly one consumer, the print surface. Every assertion about it moved there, and the print arm is the one that mattered most anyway.
Code-block chrome geometry can only be measured under emulated print media now. A display:none element measures 0 for every rect, which reported a layout fault where the CSS was untouched.
